JUBILEE: A Benchmark Environment for
Off-Policy Evaluation in Debt Collections

Diego Silva Prado diego@alphasynthesis.com Affiliation: Alpha Synthesis Labs    Tiago Amaral Penteado de Jesus tiago@alphasynthesis.com Affiliation: Alpha Synthesis Labs    Bruno Caldas de Souza caldas@alphasynthesis.com Affiliation: Alpha Synthesis Labs    Cristiano Bevitori Maffia De Oliveira cbmo@alphasynthesis.com Affiliation: Alpha Synthesis Labs
Abstract

Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value a candidate decision policy would achieve, using only data logged by the policy already in production. In debt collections, unrecorded factors can influence both actions and outcomes. This paper presents JUBILEE, a benchmark environment built around a debt-collections simulator that generates million-loan panels with competing risks, rare recovery events, and hidden factors driving both outcomes and assignment. The evaluation includes an 80-run comparison of tabular and gradient-boosted estimators under two synthetic outcome mechanisms and a 190-run parameter grid. Independent policy simulations provide reference values with estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty for a synthetic reward score and for simulated cash. With hidden factors influencing action assignment, several tabular methods agree closely while underestimating the field-visit policy’s score, an error that also appears with boosted models. Intervals from tabular doubly robust estimation usually contain the reference without hidden assignment dependence but mostly miss it when that dependence is present. Estimates from randomized decisions do not show the same large error, although their limited precision leaves policy choice uncertain. The decision consequences depend on how policy value is defined. The field-visit policy ranks last under the score and first under simulated cash, which excludes channel costs. Under cash, log-based estimators miss this best candidate in nearly every run with hidden assignment dependence in the paired study. JUBILEE supports reproducible study of these failure modes under specified collections mechanisms.

00footnotetext: The code is available at https://github.com/alpha-synthesis/jubilee
and the data at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24008544.

1 Introduction

Debt collections is becoming a reinforcement-learning domain. Discount policies are learned and deployed at a financial institution (Brandão et al. 2025). Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates a candidate policy’s value from logs generated by an incumbent. Proprietary collections records can be difficult to share (Kriebel and Yam 2020), while public credit data do not supply the counterfactual contact-and-offer outcomes needed to measure OPE error directly.

Even detailed logs can omit hardship, contactability or other information used to assign actions. The resulting confounding can make observational associations differ from intervention effects. Simulation supplies references under specified mechanisms, with precedents in healthcare and adapted MDPs (Namkoong et al. 2020; Bruns-Smith 2021; Kausik et al. 2024). Collections adds contact channels, settlement offers, rare recoveries and competing terminal events to that evaluation setting.

JUBILEE, the benchmark environment introduced in this paper, turns those failure conditions into experimental parameters. The contribution is an environment and protocol, evaluated through three complementary analyses:

  • •

    Independent reference populations quantify simulation uncertainty, including paired policy differences, so estimator error is read against reference precision.

  • •

    Under hidden coupling, tabular and gradient-boosted log-based estimators underestimate the field-visit policy by about one fifth of its score. Tabular DR intervals usually contain the reference in controls but mostly miss it under coupling. Agreement among tabular estimators is algebraic, while boosted estimators disagree in controls and coupled conditions alike. Neither pattern alone identifies the error.

  • •

    Estimators restricted to flagged randomized decisions avoid this error at about three times the interval width, and refitting the direct method (DM) exposes omitted fitting uncertainty. The underestimated policy is the worst candidate under the score and the best under simulated cash, gross of channel costs. Under cash, coupling therefore leads tabular DR to miss the best candidate in nearly every run of the paired study.

The parameters are deliberately not calibrated to any portfolio, and every claim concerns estimator behavior under known conditions. JUBILEE’s 4% recovery target controls event rarity. Results use the score defined in Section 3.1, and Section 5.8 repeats them under simulated cash. Shared seeds and fixed candidate rankings further bound generalization.

This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 presents the benchmark environment, and Section 4 describes the experimental protocol. Section 5 reports the results, while Section 6 discusses their implications and limitations. Section 7 concludes. The appendices provide configuration details, complete results and validation checks.

2 Related Work

The estimators graded here are the standard OPE toolkit. They include inverse-propensity weighting from Horvitz–Thompson theory (Horvitz and Thompson 1952), its self-normalized variant (Swaminathan and Joachims 2015), and doubly robust (DR) estimation (Dudík et al. 2011), with cross-fitted nuisances (Chernozhukov et al. 2018). JUBILEE’s contribution therefore concerns the environment and evaluation protocol.

Existing benchmarks provide infrastructure for these comparisons. COBS compares OPE estimators across RL settings (Voloshin et al. 2021), while DOPE supplies policy-dataset benchmarks (Fu et al. 2021). Open Bandit complements these resources with randomized recommendation logs (Saito et al. 2021), and SCOPE-RL supplies evaluation software (Kiyohara et al. 2023). Alongside this benchmarking work, controlled confounding has direct precedents in sequential sensitivity bounds in healthcare (Namkoong et al. 2020), model-based and model-free bounds (Bruns-Smith 2021), identification under different temporal assumptions (Kausik et al. 2024), structural counterfactual models (Oberst and Sontag 2019), and sensitivity-bound estimation for robust policy learning (Hess et al. 2026). JUBILEE’s generated-confounding parameter differs from an estimator’s sensitivity parameter.

A complementary line extends evaluation information through counterfactual annotations. Tang and Wiens (2023) augment IS, and CANDOR (Mandyam et al. 2026) develops DR variants. Following this line, JUBILEE includes annotation-augmented estimation in its panel, drawing annotations from the privileged simulator rather than from people. It also examines when the tabular estimator construction cancels their contribution.

These methodological connections also extend to finance. Simulators such as ABIDES (Byrd et al. 2020) and synthetic-data research (Assefa et al. 2020) motivate reusable environments. Within collections, prior work includes proprietary-data studies (Kriebel and Yam 2020; Brandão et al. 2025), public RL code (Yang 2019) and LendingClub-based policy simulation with recovery, costs and net profit (Sanz-Martín et al. 2026). Against this background, JUBILEE grades OPE from logged actions while varying hidden assignment, noise, exploration and annotation quality. Table 1 brings these methodological and domain antecedents together. Different objectives and temporal assumptions preclude benchmark equivalence, and the combination of simulation, controlled confounding and references carries no general priority claim.

3 The JUBILEE Benchmark Environment

JUBILEE wraps a synthetic debt-collections simulator in an evaluation protocol. Separate pathways supply logged observations, privileged annotations and policy references. The paired-study configuration is shown in Figure 1. Estimators receive observable logs, while independent simulations supply grading values. The equations in this section define JUBILEE’s synthetic model and score.

3.1 The simulated world

Each world contains one million loans. Each loan moves through a monthly state machine, from current through delinquent to late-stage delinquency, with two competing terminal events, recovery and charge-off. Both studies log 12 months for a nine-month reward window. Under the released simulator’s full-settlement rule, an accepted offer is paid in full, the discounted remainder is written off and the loan closes as cured. Actions comprise no contact, SMS, app message, phone or field visit, with offers in [0,0.55][0,0.55]. The benchmark’s decision score is written as:

ri=[recovered in months m..m+8]⋅balancei⋅(1−di)r_{i}\;=\;\mathbf{1}\!\left[\text{recovered in months }m..m{+}8\right]\cdot\text{balance}_{i}\cdot(1-d_{i}) (1)

where rir_{i} is the score for loan ii, mm is the decision month, balancei\text{balance}_{i} is the balance at that decision and did_{i} is the offered discount fraction. The indicator 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] records recovery within the nine-month window from mm through m+8m+8. The score applies that discount to any first recovery in the window, including recovery under a later offer. Continuation after the decision month is common to all candidates, so the score separates candidates largely through their initial discounts. Section 5.8 repeats the evaluation with simulated cash, the payments of months mm to m+8m+8, which under full settlement is a single payment of the balance at recovery net of the discount offered in that month. Values, errors and regrets use this US$-per-decision score unless labeled as cash. It excludes channel costs and borrower welfare and differs from payments received. The horizon and offer bound are experimental settings.

Recovery follows a logistic model whose monthly probability for decision ii is given by:

logit⁡pi=\displaystyle\operatorname{logit}p_{i}={} logit⁡(τ)+γai​(dpdi)+β⁡(1−e−κ​di)+f⁡(zi)\displaystyle\operatorname{logit}(\tau)+\gamma_{a_{i}}(\mathrm{dpd}_{i})+\beta(1-e^{-\kappa d_{i}})+f(z_{i}) (2)
+0.55​uires−0.60​uifric−0.45​mr⁡(i)\displaystyle+0.55\,u_{i}^{\mathrm{res}}-0.60\,u_{i}^{\mathrm{fric}}-0.45\,m_{r(i)}
+0.35 1[ai≠none]uicont+σξi\displaystyle+0.35\,\mathbf{1}[a_{i}\neq\mathrm{none}]\,u_{i}^{\mathrm{cont}}+\sigma\,\xi_{i}

where pip_{i} is monthly recovery probability and logit\operatorname{logit} the log-odds transform. The baseline monthly hazard is τ\tau, aia_{i} is the contact action, did_{i} its discount and dpdi\mathrm{dpd}_{i} days past due. The log-odds channel effect is γai​(dpdi)\gamma_{a_{i}}(\mathrm{dpd}_{i}), while β\beta and κ\kappa control the magnitude and saturation of the discount response. The observed covariates ziz_{i} enter through f⁡(zi)f(z_{i}), specified in Appendix A.

The components uiresu_{i}^{\mathrm{res}}, uifricu_{i}^{\mathrm{fric}} and uicontu_{i}^{\mathrm{cont}} represent resilience, payment friction and contactability. The mapping r⁡(i)r(i) selects the loan’s region and mr⁡(i)m_{r(i)} its shared shock. The term σ​ξi\sigma\xi_{i} scales a standard Gaussian log-odds shock ξi\xi_{i} by σ\sigma. The indicator activates contactability only when aia_{i} differs from none\mathrm{none}, the no-contact action. The latent factors are distributed as:

ui∼𝒩⁡(0,α2​I3),mr∼𝒩⁡(0,(0.45​α)2)u_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\,\alpha^{2}I_{3}\right),\qquad m_{r}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\,(0.45\,\alpha)^{2}\right) (3)

where 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a Gaussian distribution with mean zero, and I3I_{3} is the 3×33\times 3 identity matrix. The vector uiu_{i} collects the three independent borrower factors, each with standard deviation α\alpha. The shock mrm_{r} for region rr has standard deviation 0.45​α0.45\alpha. These distributions and coefficients are synthetic assumptions, without portfolio calibration.

A coupling switch controls whether hidden factors influence assignment. With coupling enabled, harder cases receive more contact. Disabling it retains hidden outcome variance but removes that assignment dependence, providing a negative control at the experiment’s resolution. Experimental settings are specified in Section 4.

3.2 Logging policy and exploration floor

JUBILEE defines the baseline incumbent πb\pi_{b} through its channel and discount-bin distributions. Its nominal probabilities on the action grid, before offer rounding, are written as:

πb​(a∣dpdi,si)={pb​(c∣si)​q​(k∣dpdi),a=(c,k),c≠none,pb​(none∣si),a=none\pi_{b}(a\mid\mathrm{dpd}_{i},s_{i})=\begin{cases}p_{b}(c\mid s_{i})\,q(k\mid\mathrm{dpd}_{i}),&a=(c,k),\ c\neq\mathrm{none},\\ p_{b}(\mathrm{none}\mid s_{i}),&a=\mathrm{none}\end{cases} (4)

where aa is the action for loan ii, cc its channel and kk its discount bin. The functions pbp_{b} and qq give the channel and discount-bin probabilities, respectively. Days past due are dpdi\mathrm{dpd}_{i}, and sis_{i} is dimensionless assignment intensity. The no-contact action has zero discount. With hidden coupling enabled, the benchmark’s intensity is given by:

si=clip⁡(dpdi/180+uifric− 0.4​uicont,[−2,2])s_{i}\;=\;\operatorname{clip}\!\big(\mathrm{dpd}_{i}/180\;+\;u_{i}^{\mathrm{fric}}\;-\;0.4\,u_{i}^{\mathrm{cont}},\;[-2,2]\big) (5)

where uifricu_{i}^{\mathrm{fric}} is the hidden friction factor and uicontu_{i}^{\mathrm{cont}} is the hidden contactability factor. The operator clip\operatorname{clip} truncates intensity to [−2,2][-2,2]. Higher friction or delinquency increases sis_{i}, which changes the channel probabilities through the normalized exponential weights (McFadden 1974), written as:

pb​(c∣si)=wc​exp⁡(ηc​si)∑j∈𝒞wj​exp⁡(ηj​si)p_{b}(c\mid s_{i})=\frac{w_{c}\exp(\eta_{c}s_{i})}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}}w_{j}\exp(\eta_{j}s_{i})} (6)

where wcw_{c} is the base weight and ηc\eta_{c} its intensity coefficient. The set 𝒞\mathcal{C} contains the five channels, including no contact, and jj indexes the denominator’s sum over channels. Table 18 gives their weights and coefficients. With coupling off, all ηc\eta_{c} are zero. The discount component is given by:

q⁡(k∣dpdi)=Pr⁡(Di∈Ik∣dpdi)q(k\mid\mathrm{dpd}_{i})=\Pr(D_{i}\in I_{k}\mid\mathrm{dpd}_{i}) (7)

where DiD_{i} is the offer before rounding and IkI_{k} its kk-th discount interval. Bins are five percentage points wide, with the last including the 55% cap. The offer combines a scaled Beta draw with an adjustment for delinquency. Appendix A specifies this law, expands qq and describes rounding.

Flagged randomization adds an exploration component with known assignment probabilities (Horvitz and Thompson 1952; Li et al. 2011). On explorable states, the resulting logging policy is written as:

π~b​(a∣dpdi,si)=(1−ε)​πb​(a∣dpdi,si)+ε44​ 1​[a​ active]\tilde{\pi}_{b}(a\mid\mathrm{dpd}_{i},s_{i})\;=\;(1-\varepsilon)\,\pi_{b}(a\mid\mathrm{dpd}_{i},s_{i})\;+\;\frac{\varepsilon}{44}\,\mathbf{1}[a\text{ active}] (8)

where π~b\tilde{\pi}_{b} is the logging policy with exploration, πb\pi_{b} is the baseline incumbent and ε\varepsilon the randomized share. The indicator selects active contact actions. Exploration draws a channel uniformly from the four contact channels and an independent discount uniformly on [0,0.55)[0,0.55). The eleven equal-width bins therefore give each of the 44 channel–offer cells nominal randomization probability ε/44\varepsilon/44. Explorable states comprise delinquent loans and late-stage delinquency within the eligibility limit of Section 4. Outside these states, π~b=πb\tilde{\pi}_{b}=\pi_{b}. At ε=0\varepsilon=0, pilots are undefined because no flagged randomized rows exist. This construction links hidden factors to assignment when coupling is enabled and supplies flagged randomized decisions for evaluation.

3.3 Reference values by policy simulation

JUBILEE simulates each candidate policy directly to obtain reference values for assessing OPE estimates. The candidate π\pi acts at month zero, and subsequent decisions follow the same logging policy π~b\tilde{\pi}_{b} through the nine-month window. The corresponding policy-value expectation (Dudík et al. 2011) is written as:

V(π∣M)=𝔼π,π~b[𝟏{recovered in months :8}B0(1−d0)∣initially explorable,M]V(\pi\mid M)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi,\tilde{\pi}_{b}}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{\text{recovered in months }0\!:\!8\}B_{0}(1-d_{0})\mid\text{initially explorable},M\right] (9)

where V⁡(π∣M)V(\pi\mid M) is the expected score per initially explorable loan, conditional on the regional-shock vector MM. The quantities B0B_{0} and d0d_{0} are the month-zero balance and discount, and the indicator selects first recovery in months 0–8. The expectation averages borrower and outcome variation. The reference estimates this population expectation with Monte Carlo error, rather than an exact counterfactual for the logged finite portfolio. For cash, payments in months 0–8 replace the score inside the expectation.

Both studies use independent populations for logs, annotations and reference values, conditional on common regional shocks. Within each reference replicate, candidates share borrowers, latent factors and random draws to improve the precision of their value differences. For a fixed configuration, seed, replicate and batch size, only actions and the resulting trajectories differ. Changing the batch size changes the population.

3.4 The estimator view and the data gate

The tabular view has 36 contexts, crossing capped 30-day delinquency buckets with logged-balance terciles, and 45 actions, comprising the null action and the active offer bins. Balance cut points are learned from logs and reused across reference and annotation populations. Tabular estimators use empirical within-context action frequencies computed from the logged cohort. This coarse view can leave observed assignment variation unadjusted as well as omitting hidden factors. Boosted models use richer observed covariates and cross-fitted propensity classifiers (Section 4).

A hard data gate separates what estimators may read from what grading may read. It excludes hidden factors, true recovery probabilities and the incumbent rule from estimator inputs. Privileged information supports only grading and the specified annotation procedure, keeping both separate from observational policy evaluation.

4 Experimental Protocol

The 190-run grid maps sensitivity within a tabular construction. The 80-run paired study compares tabular and boosted estimators under two outcome mechanisms, using independent references to assess precision, intervals and selection. Both evaluate the same initial-action score and simulated cash.

4.1 Parameter grid

The grid evaluates sensitivity to exploration, outcome noise and confounding through seventeen selected parameter configurations, repeated over simulation seeds for a total of 190 runs. These configurations combine confounding strength α∈{0.2,0.4,0.6,1.0,1.4,1.8}\alpha\in\{0.2,0.4,0.6,1.0,1.4,1.8\}, outcome noise σ∈{0.15,0.25,0.40,0.60}\sigma\in\{0.15,0.25,0.40,0.60\} and exploration ε∈{0,0.08}\varepsilon\in\{0,0.08\}. Along the confounding axis, σ=0.25\sigma=0.25 is held fixed, while the noise axis holds α=0.6\alpha=0.6. Two additional configurations combine higher confounding and noise, and a coupling-off control retains hidden variance at α=0.6\alpha=0.6. Together, these comparisons form the grid reported in Table 19.

To keep recovery events rare across the grid, each cell’s baseline hazard was calibrated on 50,000-borrower development worlds to an internal annual recovery target of 4.0%±0.34.0\%\pm 0.3 percentage points. Post-charge-off recovery rates and debt-purchase prices concern different events and populations (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau 2021; Federal Trade Commission 2013). Cells already within the calibration tolerance retained the strength-0.6 hazard of 0.001700, which five cells therefore share in Table 19. The stronger confounding and noise cells were retuned, while the coupling-off control’s hazard is 11% above its coupled counterpart. Under the released simulator, these hazards yield cell-mean annual recovery of 3.9 to 4.4%, with one cell above the calibration tolerance.

This recalibration affects the interpretation of comparisons across cells. Each retuned cell jointly specifies the varied parameter and its compensating baseline hazard. Consequently, exploration pairs isolate a fixed-hazard exploration effect only where both members share a hazard. Section 5.7 examines that effect separately.

Within each configuration, the target πvisit\pi_{\mathrm{visit}} assigns a visit at discount 0.275, providing a thin-support challenger, while πsms\pi_{\mathrm{sms}} assigns SMS at 0.125, closer to incumbent behavior. Both targets follow the intervention scheme of Section 3.3 on the initial explorable cohort of approximately 744,000 loans. Their offers sit at bin centers, while matching logged offers vary within bins.

Each run evaluates both targets for one configuration and simulation seed. The seven confounding-axis cells with exploration use 20 seeds each, while the remaining cells use 5. This allocation gives greater precision to the confounding comparison. With 20 seeds, the pilots’ seed-level dispersions of 46–86 US$ imply approximate 80%-power detection thresholds of 29–54 US$ at the 5% level, conditional on those dispersions. Seeds are shared across cells, preserving regional-shock dependence without guaranteeing identical portfolios. To assess estimation error within each run, three independent million-borrower reference populations provide the comparison values in Table 19, following the reference design detailed in Section 4.2.

4.2 Paired design and reference precision

The paired design compares experimental conditions using shared simulated populations and random draws, so differences can be assessed within the same seed block. Each block contains worlds A and B with assignment coupling off and on. Within each condition, tabular and gradient-boosted estimators use the same logged data and policy references. The same simulated trajectories are also evaluated under both the synthetic score and simulated cash. Independent reference populations provide policy values and quantify their Monte Carlo uncertainty, with candidate policies paired within each population.

4.2.1 Worlds, candidates and shared seed blocks

The paired study crosses worlds A and B with the assignment coupling defined in Section 3.1 switched off and on, using α=1\alpha=1, σ=0.25\sigma=0.25 and ε=0.08\varepsilon=0.08. When coupling is on, intensity sis_{i} affects the channel probabilities, whereas with coupling off, the coefficients ηc\eta_{c} are set to zero and channels follow the base weights wcw_{c}. This switch controls whether hidden factors influence channel assignment, while retaining their effects on recovery in both conditions.

In world A, channel effects are fixed across delinquency stages, and the baseline hazard is the grid’s strength-1.0 value, held fixed across coupling conditions. By contrast, world B has stage-dependent active-channel effects that change at 90 days past due. Its baseline hazard is calibrated in development to match A’s annual recovery rate and is also held fixed across coupling conditions within B. Table 2 reports the log-odds channel effects and monthly baseline hazards. These are synthetic mechanism contrasts, without estimated real-world channel efficacy.

Because the coupling switch also changes observed delinquency tilt, action support and incumbent continuation, on–off contrasts do not isolate a pure change in hidden information. For these comparisons, twenty seeds form paired blocks across all four conditions, sharing populations, latent factors, regional shocks and random draws. Within each coupling condition, worlds A/B also share initial logged actions. The 80 runs comprise 20 independent blocks, with disjoint development seeds.

Policy selection in these blocks compares the incumbent πb\pi_{b}, the two constant targets and πstage\pi_{\mathrm{stage}}, which assigns SMS at discount 0.025 before 90 days past due and a visit at 0.275 thereafter. All challengers use the intervention scheme in Section 3.3, and eligibility requires initial delinquency or late-stage delinquency of at most 180 days. The stage boundary aligns with the tabular context. These candidates and eligibility rules are experimental settings, without operational optimality claims.

4.2.2 Reference precision and analysis

For these comparisons, each run uses three independent million-borrower reference populations, conditional on common regional shocks, with candidates paired within populations. A development pilot selects the smallest replicate count meeting per-run Monte Carlo standard-error (SE) targets of 2.0 US$ for values and 1.0 US$ for paired gaps within the compute ceiling. For policy comparisons, a best-versus-runner-up gap exceeding 1.96 paired reference SEs is labeled resolved as a pointwise precision diagnostic, without simultaneous winner guarantees. Variation across seed blocks is reported separately from this Monte Carlo uncertainty.

Using these references, errors are defined as estimates minus references. Mean error and root-mean-square error (RMSE) describe their direction and magnitude, while intervals are graded by reference containment, distinct from coverage of an expected value. Policy choice is assessed by score regret, the best reference value minus that of the selected candidate. For the incumbent, the logged mean supplies its selection estimate, and independent references supply its grading value. All runs are retained in these analyses, including extremes.

The configuration and planned analyses were fixed before execution and are supplied with the code. The cash analyses were specified after an exploratory comparison had ranked the field visit first under cash and before the simulations reported here. In contrast, spread, replicate-consistency checks, top-two decompositions, selection tests and differences-in-differences are post hoc. For the selection tests, paired seed-block mean regret differences are compared against zero, with Holm adjustment across the twelve tt-tests of each objective (Holm 1979). Of these, nine compare pilot-IS, pilot-DR and boosted DR with tabular DR, pooling over all conditions, controls only or coupled conditions only. The remaining three compare tabular DR’s regret with coupling on against off, separately in A, in B and over both worlds.

4.3 Estimators and evaluation measures

The panel contains six log-based and two exploration-based estimators (Table 3). Family statements exclude context-blind DM.

The direct-method estimator follows Dudík et al. (2011), written as:

V^DM=1n​∑i∑aπe​(a∣xi)​R^​(xi,a)\hat{V}_{\mathrm{DM}}=\tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_{i}\sum_{a}\pi_{e}(a\mid x_{i})\,\hat{R}(x_{i},a) (10)

where V^DM\hat{V}_{\mathrm{DM}} is the policy-value estimate over nn cohort rows indexed by ii. The observed context is xix_{i}, aa ranges over available actions, πe​(a∣xi)\pi_{e}(a\mid x_{i}) is the target action probability and R^​(xi,a)\hat{R}(x_{i},a) the predicted score. The importance-sampling estimator (Horvitz and Thompson 1952; Dudík et al. 2011) is given by:

V^IS=1n​∑iρi​ri\hat{V}_{\mathrm{IS}}=\tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_{i}\rho_{i}\,r_{i} (11)

where rir_{i} is the logged score for action aia_{i}, and ρi=πe​(ai∣xi)/P^​(ai∣xi)\rho_{i}=\pi_{e}(a_{i}\mid x_{i})/\hat{P}(a_{i}\mid x_{i}) is its importance weight. The denominator P^​(ai∣xi)\hat{P}(a_{i}\mid x_{i}) estimates the logging probability from observed context. The cohort size nn and contexts xix_{i} follow Equation (10). SNIPS normalizes by the sum of weights (Swaminathan and Joachims 2015). Combining model predictions with weighted residuals gives the doubly robust estimator (Dudík et al. 2011), written as:

V^DR=1n​∑i[∑aπe​(a∣xi)​R^​(xi,a)+ρi​(ri−R^​(xi,ai))]\hat{V}_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_{i}\Big[\sum_{a}\pi_{e}(a\mid x_{i})\,\hat{R}(x_{i},a)+\rho_{i}\big(r_{i}-\hat{R}(x_{i},a_{i})\big)\Big] (12)

where ri−R^​(xi,ai)r_{i}-\hat{R}(x_{i},a_{i}) is the prediction residual for the logged action. The other symbols retain their definitions from Equations (10) and (11). The estimator combines the DM prediction average with the importance-weighted residual correction. Its guarantees require identification and support, which hidden confounding can invalidate. In the tabular construction, empirical propensities and a shared 36-by-45 reward grid make DM, IS and SNIPS algebraically identical when every occupied context supports the target. With these propensities the importance-weighted model term equals the DM term for any reward model, so the DR correction vanishes and DR reduces to IS whatever the reward model, including the annotation-augmented model of Equation (13). Cross-fitting and empty-cell handling explain the small differences between methods.

Pilot estimators use the decisions randomized by the exploration component, whose assignment probabilities are known. Following the design in Equation (8), both use weight 44/ε44/\varepsilon only on flagged randomized rows matching the target and retain the full cohort denominator. Pilot-IS weights observed scores, whereas pilot-DR weights prediction residuals and also averages model predictions over the full cohort.

The annotation-augmented reward-model fit follows CANDOR (Mandyam et al. 2026), using logged and weighted annotation rows as:

R^+=fit on​{(xi,ai,ri)}⏟logged rows∪{(x,aπe​(x),r~x)}⏟annotations, weight ​ω\hat{R}^{+}\;=\;\text{fit on}\;\;\underbrace{\{(x_{i},\,a_{i},\,r_{i})\}}_{\text{logged rows}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\{(x,\,a^{\pi_{e}}(x),\,\tilde{r}_{x})\}}_{\text{annotations, weight }\omega} (13)

where R^+\hat{R}^{+} is the annotation-augmented reward model. The union combines logged context–action–score triplets with annotation rows. For an annotation, xx is its context, aπe​(x)a^{\pi_{e}}(x) the target action, r~x\tilde{r}_{x} its annotated score and ω\omega its fitting weight. Both studies draw annotations from an independent population and add bias and Gaussian noise at 0.25 of the maximum absolute cell reward, with unit annotation weight. The auxiliary bandit uses a perfect annotator. Annotations enter only the reward-model fit in Equation (12), so under the tabular propensities above they cannot move the DM+-IS estimate beyond cross-fitting noise and unsupported cells. CANDOR’s bias guarantee for this construction requires exact importance ratios, which only the auxiliary bandit has. The annotated direct method DM+ averages R^+\hat{R}^{+} over the cohort as in Equation (10), without the residual correction, so annotations act on it directly.

4.4 Gradient-boosted nuisances and inference

The paired study evaluates DM, IS, SNIPS, DR and pilot-DR with histogram gradient boosting implemented in scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011). Reward models use the action and 15 observed loan and borrower attributes. Target-specific classifiers estimate matching-action probabilities. Both nuisances use two-fold cross-fitting (Chernozhukov et al. 2018). Tabular models use coarse contexts and full-cohort empirical propensities, cross-fitting only the reward model. The comparison therefore changes covariates and fitting alongside model class.

A reference-free development rule compares the library default with a regularized configuration by the largest deviation of the mean IS weight from unity across targets, keeps the smaller deviation and prefers the default in a near tie. The regularized configuration was selected, with 300 iterations, learning rate 0.05, at most 15 leaves, at least 1,000 rows per leaf and unit L2L_{2} regularization. Propensities are clipped at 0.001, below the design floor ε/44\varepsilon/44, and Appendix B reports support, clipped counts and mean weights. Pilot-IS is shared across regimes, and annotation augmentation is tabular only.

Bootstrap resampling follows Efron (1979). Both designs use nominal 90% percentile intervals from 200 borrower resamples, conditional on regional shocks. Fixed-model DM resamples predictions, omitting fitting uncertainty. IS/SNIPS resample weighted outcomes, DR/augmented DR resample fixed-nuisance contributions, and pilots use design-weighted contributions. The DM diagnostic refits its model in each resample. Reference uncertainty is separate. Auxiliary exploration intervals instead use Student intervals for seed-level means.

All the experiments presented in this section have their computational costs summarized here. The grid used 140.8 CPU-hours, about 44 minutes per run. Reference sizing and the paired study used 17.4 and 94.2 CPU-hours, the latter including estimation under both objectives. Untimed supporting diagnostics are estimated at 10–20 CPU-hours, separately from measured auxiliary costs in Appendix C.

5 Results

All runs specified in Section 4 have results reported here. The analysis first checks reference precision and negative controls (Section 5.1), then compares estimator errors and agreement under hidden coupling (Section 5.2). Estimator precision under randomized exploration (Section 5.3), model misspecification and interval construction (Section 5.4), and annotation quality (Section 5.5) are examined before policy selection and score regret (Section 5.6). The final analyses measure exploration’s effect on the incumbent score (Section 5.7) and assess rankings and decisions under simulated cash (Section 5.8).

Auxiliary bandit and annotator experiments are identified separately. Errors are estimates minus simulated references, reported as means with one seed-level SE in US$ per decision. They include reference Monte Carlo variation. Values and regrets use the score in Equation (1) unless labeled as cash.

5.1 Reference precision and negative controls

In the paired study, reference SEs meet the targets in every run, with maxima of 1.88 US$ for values and 0.61 US$ for gaps. Table 4 averages 20 seeds per condition, sharing blocks across conditions. The stage policy is reference-best in every run, with a minimum runner-up gap of 12.2 US$. The winner is unchanged when grading uses one, two or three reference populations.

The incumbent’s logged-minus-reference mean ranges from −0.08-0.08 to +0.58+0.58 US$, with SEs of 0.71–0.83 US$. The coupling-off conditions serve as negative controls, retaining hidden outcome variation while disabling its direct influence on channel assignment. These controls show no detectable mean error for the context-conditioned tabular family, boosted DR/SNIPS or pilots. Boosted DM and IS have control errors (Table 24). Pilot mean-error 95% intervals extend 23 to 39 US$ on either side of zero, leaving smaller biases unresolved. A post hoc check finds less reference-mean dispersion than predicted for values, with unresolved cause (Appendix C.1).

The grid’s coupling-off control likewise shows no detectable mean error (Table 5, ε=0.08\varepsilon=0.08, 20 seeds). Its approximate 80%-power resolution at the 5% level is 11 to 16 US$ for log-based methods and 37–53 US$ for pilots, and grid reference SEs are at most 1.97 US$ per run. Passing this check does not establish zero bias.

5.2 Errors under confounded assignment

Across individual grid runs, target-policy reference scores span 203–419 US$ per decision, with cell means in Table 19. With coupling enabled, the visit-policy error grows with α\alpha (Table 6, Figure 2). Each plotted cell has ε=0.08\varepsilon=0.08 and 20 seeds, with bars of one SE. The control retains α=0.6\alpha=0.6 with coupling off. Five context-conditioned methods agree within 0.3 US$ for visits and 0.7 US$ for SMS, so DR represents them in the table and one curve represents them in the figure. Context-blind DM is separate. This agreement follows the tabular algebra of Section 4 and does not establish accuracy.

Visit errors are −7.9±3.9-7.9\pm 3.9 and −14.2±3.8-14.2\pm 3.8 US$ at strengths 0.2 and 0.4, roughly double between 0.4 and 0.6, and reach −120.7±5.2-120.7\pm 5.2 US$ at 1.8. That is 44% of the cell’s 274.0 US$ reference value. SMS remains within one SE of zero throughout, using a tighter plot scale. The noise sweep (σ=0.15\sigma=0.15–0.600.60, strength 0.6) shows no ordered DR-error trend, with interval widths of 60–63 US$. Its 5-seed cells have SEs of 6 to 8 US$, so differences between cells below roughly 30 US$ are unresolved, limiting generalization about noise.

The paired study retains a visit-policy underestimation of approximately one fifth under coupling (Table 7, mean error ±\pm one SE over 20 seeds). Boosted DM, DR and SNIPS share errors of a similar scale. Boosted IS is less negative because it carries a positive offset of 9 to 14 US$ on every target in the controls, where its mean importance weight exceeds one, so its on–off contrast matches the others. Boosted DM errs by −9.3±1.5-9.3\pm 1.5 and −14.2±1.3-14.2\pm 1.3 US$ on the stage policy in the controls, an error that the DR correction removes. Pilot errors are compatible with zero at wider uncertainty, and the RMSE comparison in Appendix B shows no uniform pilot advantage.

An exploratory within-run spread, the largest minus smallest log-based estimate, averages 0.6–2.0 US$ for tabular methods and 18–29 US$ for boosted methods, or 12–25 US$ without boosted IS, including controls (Table 23). Thus disagreement also occurs without hidden coupling, while coupled boosted methods can still share downward error. Figure 3 compares tabular DR, boosted DR and pilot-IS on a common scale, with one-SE bars over shared seed blocks. Full results and additional paired contrasts appear in the appendices.

World B moves values and gaps without changing their ordering. Its coupled tabular-DR visit error differs from A by only +0.8±1.8+0.8\pm 1.8 US$. Grid cell 06 shares the configuration of condition AonA_{\mathrm{on}} with different seeds, and the two agree on the reference scores within 0.4 US$ and on the tabular DR visit error within one SE, −61.4±2.6-61.4\pm 2.6 against −57.5±3.8-57.5\pm 3.8 US$.

5.3 Identification from randomized exploration

Pilots use flagged randomization rather than estimated logging propensities. In the control and at every coupled strength of the 20-seed ladder, neither pilot deviates from zero by more than one SE, while log-based error reaches −120.7-120.7 US$ (Table 6).

Without exploration the pilots are undefined in five cells. With ε=0.08\varepsilon=0.08, approximately 59,000 decisions are randomized, but only 1,277 to 1,453 per run match a given target in the grid, and 1,279 to 1,425 in the paired study. Their visit-policy 90% intervals are 2.7–3.1 times wider than DR’s on the noise ladder, at 168–186 US$ against 60–63 US$.

5.4 Self-evaluation and interval construction

A contextual bandit isolates reward-model misspecification using exact propensities and a perfect annotator, with target value 0.3327 per unit of debt, N=2000N=2000 logged decisions per seed, ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1 and 200 seeds. The well-specified model conditions on context and action, while the misspecified model uses actions alone. In Table 8, all well-specified biases are within about one Monte Carlo SE of zero. Misspecified DM loses 0.1476±0.00290.1476\pm 0.0029, or 44% of truth, while importance-corrected estimates remain compatible with zero.

DM+-IS has the lowest RMSE in both regimes. Shared-seed squared-error comparisons yield paired tt-statistics of at least 2.7 when well-specified and 3.8 when misspecified (n=200n=200 seeds). This is pairwise evidence under a perfect annotator, not a recommendation for unknown annotation quality.

The grid also distinguishes point estimates from interval construction (Table 9). All methods use the same 165 runs, excluding 25 without exploration. The fractions pool cells of every confounding strength, so the visit column mixes near-zero and large errors, and Tables 10 and 11 separate control from coupled conditions. Fractions describe nominal 90% reference containment and widths are in US$ per decision. IS/SNIPS contain about half the visit references and 86% of SMS references despite point values close to DM. Fixed-model DM intervals omit fitting uncertainty and fail even in controls. Context-blind DM intervals are degenerate.

In the 20-run control of Table 10 (ε=0.08\varepsilon=0.08), DR and refitted DM intervals contain the reference in 18 or 19 runs, whereas fixed-model DM intervals contain none. Pilots contain more pooled visit references at about three times the width. Shared seeds prevent treating pooled fractions as independent binomial observations, and none incorporates reference error.

Refitting tabular DM within bootstrap resamples widens intervals (Table 11, containment counts out of 20 with mean full widths in parentheses). Control widths imply bootstrap SDs close to across-seed error SDs for visits and stage policies, and 30–35% larger for SMS, with only 19 degrees of freedom. Refit intervals contain control references in 18–19 runs, but coupled visit references in only 2 per world. Fixed-nuisance DR intervals have similar widths and the same containment pattern, 17 to 19 of 20 in the controls and 2 of 20 for the coupled visit policy. Twenty runs per condition cannot establish precise nominal coverage.

5.5 Annotator fidelity

Under tabular empirical propensities, the importance-weighted correction cancels the reward model (Section 4), and DM+-IS stays within 0.3 US$ of IS in the paired study whatever the annotations.

To examine annotation quality without this cancellation, the annotated direct method DM+ is evaluated with exact and corrupted annotations (Table 12, field-visit policy, score). Exact annotations are context means of the target policy’s own outcomes in the independent annotation population, one per logged row. With exact annotations, DM+’s error lies between −0.8-0.8 and +0.1+0.1 US$ for every condition, target and objective, including the coupled visit policy whose log-based error is −57.5±3.8-57.5\pm 3.8 US$.

With the specified corruption, whose bias is 0.25 of the largest cell reward, DM+’s error instead rises to +150+150 to +243+243 US$.

5.6 Policy selection and score regret

A post hoc grid analysis selects the highest estimated value among the incumbent and two targets, grading against realized references on the same 165 runs. Table 13 reports correct counts and mean score regret in US$ per decision. SMS is reference-best in all 190 runs. Because the same candidate wins every run, a constant choice would have zero regret, and the counts measure how often estimation error displaces a fixed winner. Context-conditioned log-based methods have lower observed regret than pilots, and context-blind DM has the lowest. Configuration-level values and choices appear in Tables 19 and 20.

The paired study adds the stage challenger, which is reference-best in every run. All five context-conditioned tabular methods make identical choices. Table 14 gives correct selections out of 20 and mean score regret ±\pm one SE in parentheses, comparing their DR representative with boosted DR and tabular pilots. Pilots have higher observed regret in every condition. Most incorrect log-based choices select SMS. Selection errors also occur in controls.

An exploratory comparison helps explain these selection errors. Under coupling, the stage-minus-SMS error is −17.5±7.3-17.5\pm 7.3 US$ in A and −15.5±7.4-15.5\pm 7.4 US$ in B, against reference gaps of 13.2 and 15.6 US$. The expected estimated gap is therefore close to zero, and correct selections fall from 12 and 15 of 20 in the controls to 8 and 10. Twenty blocks leave this displacement unresolved as a reversal.

The regret tests likewise limit the selection conclusions. Under the score, none of the twelve post hoc tests survives Holm adjustment, with a minimum adjusted p=0.25p=0.25, so a general regret advantage is unestablished. Reference precision has little effect on the reported mean regret. Using fewer reference populations changes mean regret by at most 0.14 US$, while retaining the winner. True rankings remain fixed within each study.

5.7 Exploration and the score objective

A fixed-hazard comparison changes incumbent exploration from ε=0\varepsilon=0 to 0.080.08 throughout the nine-month window, unlike the intervention defined in Section 3.3. Each of 20 shared seed blocks uses a paired million-borrower population, with sizing and precision rules fixed in development. Table 15 gives Δ=V⁡(ε=0)−V⁡(ε=0.08)\Delta=V(\varepsilon=0)-V(\varepsilon=0.08) and 95% tt intervals across seeds, plus mean relative reductions. Here V⁡(ε)V(\varepsilon) is the expected incumbent score under exploration share ε\varepsilon. Positive differences in both worlds indicate a lower score under exploration. The score-equivalence result in Appendix C applies to this comparison. Full-settlement cash effects of exploration have not been evaluated.

5.8 Score and simulated cash

Because policy rankings depend on the objective, the cash analysis examines whether estimation errors lead to choosing candidates that recover less money in the simulator. Both studies repeat every estimate, interval and selection on the same simulations using the cash objective defined in Section 3.1.

The field-visit policy becomes reference-best in all 80 paired runs (Table 16) and in all 190 grid runs. In the paired study, its mean margin is 5.8 to 15.9 US$ per decision, while reference SEs reach at most 1.31 US$ for values and 0.44 US$ for paired gaps. Cash also excludes channel costs.

Despite the new ranking, the visit-policy error persists. Under coupling, tabular DR’s cash errors are −49.6±3.5-49.6\pm 3.5 and −49.1±3.2-49.1\pm 3.2 US$ in A and B, about 22% of its value. Boosted DR’s errors are −47.3±3.8-47.3\pm 3.8 and −46.4±3.7-46.4\pm 3.7 US$, while pilot errors remain compatible with zero (Appendix B.2). Tabular DR intervals again contain the coupled visit reference in 2 of 20 runs per world.

The corresponding policy choices appear in Table 17. Coupling raises tabular DR’s cash regret by 6.3±1.26.3\pm 1.2 US$ per decision over both worlds, with Holm-adjusted p<0.001p<0.001, and lowers its correct selections from 11 and 8 of 20 to 1 and 0.

Pilots select the visit policy more often, in 4 to 7 of 20 coupled runs. Their observed regret is 2.7 and 3.6 US$ below tabular DR’s for pilot-IS and pilot-DR, but these differences do not survive Holm adjustment (adjusted p=0.33p=0.33 and 0.19). The grid shows a similar selection pattern. Log-based estimators select the cash-best candidate in 33 or 34 of the 165 runs with exploration, none of them at strengths of 1.0 and above, and pilots in 66 or 68. Appendix A reports the confounding ladder and selection under cash.

6 Discussion and Limitations

JUBILEE quantifies OPE failure modes under the specified collections mechanisms. Tabular agreement coexists with large errors, while boosted methods disagree in both controls and coupled conditions. Neither pattern alone establishes accuracy.

The larger visit-policy error is consistent with the assignment mechanism in Section 3.2. Higher hidden friction and lower contactability reduce recovery while increasing assignment intensity, making visits more likely for borrowers with adverse characteristics unavailable to log-based estimators. This selection helps explain the downward visit error. SMS has no direct intensity effect on its channel weight, although normalization can still induce confounding. The smaller SMS error is specific to the tested settings, and the different candidate discounts preclude attributing the entire contrast to channel selection.

Counterfactual annotations offer additional information for reward prediction. DM+-IS trains its model on logged outcomes and annotations, then corrects its value estimate with importance-weighted differences between observed and predicted rewards. With correct ratios, identification and support, this correction offsets model error in expectation, as in conventional DR (Dudík et al. 2011; Mandyam et al. 2026). Better predictions can reduce variability, although imperfect annotations can increase it. The auxiliary bandit’s exact propensities and perfect annotator provide favorable conditions for the lower RMSE observed in both model specifications (Section 5.4).

In the coupled collections experiments, however, observed-covariate propensities lack that exact-ratio guarantee. The tabular empirical ratios also cancel the model terms, leaving DM+-IS nearly identical to IS even with annotations (Section 5.5). DM+, which uses predictions without residual correction, instead inherits the accuracy or bias of the annotations dominating its fit. Its near-reference result with exact annotations reflects privileged target-policy outcomes, and corrupted annotations transfer bias to its predictions. Thus annotation quality and estimator construction jointly determine the benefit. Because these annotations use controlled simulator outcomes, human annotator performance remains untested. The contrast between the bandit and collections shows that robustness to reward-model misspecification does not imply robustness to hidden confounding.

Known randomization supplies an alternative source of information, as in microrandomized trials (Klasnja et al. 2015). Pilots avoid the large visit error at the experiment’s resolution, but rare rewards and few matching randomized decisions limit precision. This limit and the approximation from binning continuous offers leave smaller pilot biases unresolved.

These precision limits carry into policy selection (Section 5.6). Selection depends on relative estimates, so shared shifts can preserve rankings while differential errors can change a close comparison. Under the score, the largest error penalizes an already inferior visit policy, whereas the stage–SMS error erodes the leading candidate’s advantage. Pilot variability can also change the winner, explaining why smaller mean error need not improve selection. Fixed reference winners further restrict the range of decision changes tested by these designs.

Randomization also changes the incumbent’s score (Section 5.7). The observed reduction combines changes in channels and offers under the score’s initial-discount convention, without isolating their individual contributions. Since the comparison excludes information value and has not been repeated for full-settlement cash, it does not establish the economic cost of exploration.

The cash comparison makes the objective’s role in policy selection explicit (Section 5.8). For loans unrecovered initially under both candidates, common continuation produces identical subsequent cash trajectories. The score still weights these recoveries by each candidate’s initial discount, favoring lower offers. Under simulated cash, visits become the best candidate, so the shared downward error now makes log-based estimators discard the winner. The increase in tabular DR’s cash regret under coupling is resolved, whereas regret differences between pilots and log-based estimators remain unresolved under both objectives. These contrasts support reporting error, uncertainty and choices together without a universal estimator recommendation.

Interpreting these comparisons also requires distinguishing uncertainty in model fitting from uncertainty in grading. The DM refit diagnostic exposes omitted fitting variability while retaining coupled point error, without invalidating all fixed-nuisance DR intervals. Separately, independent reference populations separate grading from logs and annotations, and pairing improves gap precision, but their SEs remain conditional on regional shocks.

Generalization is further limited by the tested mechanisms. The worlds vary one channel-effect mechanism with shared seed blocks, while latent weights, distributions, alternative clipping and bootstrap budgets lack broad sensitivity analysis. The coupling switch also changes observed assignment, support and continuation, while grid hazard recalibration changes the outcome model alongside each stress parameter. These contrasts therefore do not isolate universal confounding thresholds. Likewise, the boosted comparison changes covariates and propensity cross-fitting alongside model class, preventing separate attribution. The panel also excludes confounding-aware and sensitivity methods (Namkoong et al. 2020; Bruns-Smith 2021; Kausik et al. 2024; Hess et al. 2026).

Finally, the absence of external portfolios and the omission of channel costs and borrower welfare limit operational interpretation. Contact intensity toward distressed borrowers is also subject to consumer-protection rules, adding constraints beyond the recovery outcomes evaluated here. The supported scope is therefore a synthetic initial-action evaluation, without operational collections recommendations or full sequential-policy claims. Within this scope, JUBILEE connects estimator errors to information conditions and policy choices through reproducible experiments.

7 Conclusion

JUBILEE provides a reproducible environment for investigating when OPE failure modes arise, quantifying their magnitude and assessing their effects on policy choice under specified collections mechanisms.

The experiments show that estimator agreement can coexist with substantial error. Assessing reliability therefore requires examining uncertainty as well as point estimates, including the fitting variability omitted by fixed-model DM intervals. This uncertainty also affects policy choice. Estimates based on randomized decisions do not show the large underestimation observed in the coupled logs, but their variability across runs limits their ability to distinguish candidates. A smaller error on average therefore does not necessarily lead to more accurate policy selection in individual runs.

The evaluation objective further determines how estimation error affects that choice. Under the synthetic score, the visit policy is not the best candidate. Under simulated cash, it becomes the best, yet log-based estimators continue to underestimate its value. This underestimation can make another candidate appear preferable and lead to the selection of a policy with lower simulated cash recovery.

The simulator and evaluation protocol are available at https://github.com/alpha-synthesis/jubilee, and the cohort extracts of every run at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24008544.

The 17 grid configurations are listed in Table 19, together with calibrated monthly hazards τ\tau, run counts, realized annual recovery, mean reference scores in US$ per decision and the largest reference SE of each cell. The control has α=0.6\alpha=0.6 with coupling off. Incumbent values include exploration.

For these configurations, Table 20 reports correct choices and mean score regret in parentheses, using each cell’s run count as denominator. “–” means undefined. Cells share seeds, and the common comparison excludes configurations without exploration. The bandit and annotation diagnostics are separate from the 190-run aggregates.

Every grid run is graded by three independent million-borrower reference populations, as in the paired study. Under simulated cash, Tables 21 and 22 repeat the confounding ladder and the selection analysis. The visit policy is reference-best in every run, and log-based errors keep the sign and growth of the score’s.

Appendix B Complete results for the paired study

The complete comparisons in Tables 24, 25, 26 and 27 cover every fitted estimator in both regimes. They report mean score errors and seed-level standard errors in US$ per decision against independent simulated references, using 20 seeds per condition. Comparing regimes requires accounting for their joint changes in covariates, model class and propensity cross-fitting. Pilot-IS is shared across regimes, and shared seed blocks remain the unit for paired comparisons.

Complementing these error comparisons, Table 23 reports within-regime disagreement among log-based methods. The exploratory spread is the largest minus smallest estimate within a run, in US$ per decision, averaged over 20 blocks per condition. For the tabular regime it includes DM, IS, SNIPS, DR and augmented DR, while the boosted comparison includes DM, IS, SNIPS and DR. The third row of each condition repeats the boosted spread without IS, whose positive control offset accounts for much of the disagreement.

Table 28 reports root-mean-square error with a bootstrap-over-seeds SE for the representative estimators of both regimes and the pilots. Under coupling the pilots have no uniformly lower RMSE than the log-based estimators for the visit policy, because their seed-level dispersion is of the same order as the log-based error, and their RMSE is larger for the SMS and stage policies.

B.1 Numerical approximations and support

Targets use discount-bin centers, whereas matching logged offers vary within the bin. A development comparison of the center dose against a uniform dose within the bin changes SMS and visit values by approximately 0.03 and 0.08 US$ per decision.

A complementary first-order calculation holds recovery probabilities fixed and includes the reward factor (1−d)(1-d), weighted by context. The resulting logged-dose offsets are approximately +0.45+0.45 US$ for the visit target, −0.44-0.44 US$ for SMS and −1.97-1.97 US$ for the stage-dependent target. Because this offset calculation excludes the recovery response to dose, it is not a complete bound on discretization error.

The action-support check finds target cells in every occupied context except a small set of extreme-delinquency contexts containing at most 0.07% of the cohort. Randomized target matches range from 1,279 to 1,425 per run. Boosted estimated propensities are clipped at 0.001, below the design floor ε/44≃0.0018\varepsilon/44\simeq 0.0018. Table 29 reports, per condition and target, the logged rows matching the target, the randomized matches, the contexts without support and their cohort share, the matched rows whose estimated propensity fell below the clip, the minimum estimated propensity and the mean boosted IS weight, whose excess over one is the Jensen inflation behind the positive boosted IS control error. Neither regime receives borrower-level latent factors.

B.2 Results under simulated cash

Tables 30, 31 and 32 give mean cash errors and seed-level SEs in US$ per decision for the estimators of Table 7, against independent cash references from the same simulations as the score. Table 33 repeats the interval diagnostic under cash. Boosted IS keeps its positive control offset, and the coupled visit error of the log-based estimators is close to its score counterpart.

Appendix C Score equivalence and auxiliary analyses

The auxiliary checks examine reference precision, paired error contrasts and score equivalence between simulator models.

C.1 Reference precision and paired contrasts

A post hoc comparison of reference-replicate spread against individual-loan SE predictions gives variance ratios of 0.53–0.82 for values and 0.66–1.30 for paired gaps. Smaller-population checks found no stream or variance-formula defect. In the grid’s 20-seed cells, which use the same reference design, the value ratios are 1.03–1.41, so the lower paired-study value dispersion remains unexplained and is not a general property of the references. In the paired study, reported value SEs exceed the observed spread, without independently establishing exact calibration.

For the same seed blocks, the paired on–off visit-error contrast for tabular DR is −56.4±3.9-56.4\pm 3.9 US$ in A and −52.7±4.0-52.7\pm 4.0 US$ in B. Boosted DR gives −51.4±4.6-51.4\pm 4.6 and −46.5±4.7-46.5\pm 4.7 US$. Covariates and nuisance fitting change jointly with model class, preventing separate attribution.

C.2 Simulator-score equivalence

Model 2.0.0 permits partial payment and residual balances. Model 2.1.0 pays the full offer and closes the loan. Until first recovery, their configured streams and event probabilities are identical. The score, initial covariates, actions, annotations and references read nothing after that event, and fitting/bootstrap seeds are unchanged. Equivalence holds for the candidate policies of this study, which act at month zero and read nothing after first recovery. Tools that consume draws after a recovery are outside the argument.

To verify this score-equivalence argument, isolated comparisons cover the first two batches of eight million-borrower worlds, four conditions and two seeds, with exploration on/off, all roles and candidates, both reference windows (9 and 12 months) and the database-generation path (Table 34). All 80 complete runs were then regenerated under 2.1.0, and every estimation, reference and selection field of their score panels equals the 2.0.0 output, so the reported paired-study scores hold under the released model. Counts are array/field/summary comparisons, not independent experiments.

Analyses that read the full panel after a recovery must use the model under which the panel was generated.

The exploration-score comparison determines its replicate count on development seeds and evaluates shared confirmation seeds. Measured CPU-hours for the auxiliary analyses, including development diagnostics not reported here, are given in Table 35, excluding the main studies and untimed diagnostics.
